Exercise A

Stereotypes & Cultural Awareness – Reading

Read the text carefully, then answer the comprehension questions below by choosing the correct option.

Reading Text

Stereotypes are simplified ideas or beliefs about a particular group of people. They are often based on generalisations — for example, the idea that all Germans are punctual, all British people drink tea constantly, or all Australians love surfing. While some stereotypes may contain a grain of truth, they rarely reflect the full picture. Every person is an individual, and reducing someone to a stereotype ignores their unique personality, interests, and experiences.

Stereotypes are formed in many ways. Young children often pick up stereotypes from their families, friends, and the media. Films, television shows, and social media can reinforce stereotypes by showing certain groups of people in a limited or one-sided way. For example, indigenous peoples in countries like Canada, Australia, and New Zealand are sometimes portrayed as if they still live exactly as their ancestors did centuries ago, while their modern achievements in science, art, and politics are ignored.

Stereotypes can lead to prejudice and discrimination. When people are judged based on stereotypes rather than as individuals, it can cause real harm. In schools, students from certain backgrounds may face bullying or exclusion because of assumptions about their culture, religion, or language. In the workplace, stereotypes can affect who gets hired or promoted. Research has shown that job applicants with foreign-sounding names sometimes receive fewer interview invitations, even when their qualifications are identical to those of other candidates.

However, there are effective ways to challenge stereotypes. Travel, reading, and having conversations with people from different backgrounds can help break down false assumptions. In many countries, schools now teach about cultural diversity and encourage students to question their own biases. Exchange programmes between countries — for example between Germany and Commonwealth nations such as Canada, India, or New Zealand — give young people the chance to experience other cultures first-hand and discover that stereotypes rarely tell the whole story.

Exercise B

Passive Voice – Stereotypes & Prejudice

Choose the correct passive voice form for each sentence. Remember: passive = form of "be" + past participle. Think carefully about the tense!

Grammar reminder

Present simple passive: Stereotypes are created by the media.

Past simple passive: The students were taught about cultural diversity.

Present perfect passive: Many stereotypes have been challenged in recent years.

Present progressive passive: New programmes are being developed right now.

Fill in the Gaps

1 Stereotypes by films and television shows.

2 In many schools, cultural awareness as part of the regular curriculum right now.

3 Last year, several students because of stereotypes about their religion.

4 People from other countries based on stereotypes alone.

5 The exchange programme between our school and a school in Canada by both schools together in 2023.

6 Many false assumptions about indigenous peoples through the media over the past decades.

7 Right now, new anti-discrimination laws in the European Parliament.

8 Job applicants with foreign-sounding names because of unconscious bias.

Exercise C

If-Clauses Type III – What Could Have Been Different?

Complete the sentences using if-clauses type III. Remember: If + past perfect → would have + past participle. These describe hypothetical situations in the past — things that did NOT happen.

Grammar reminder

Type III (unreal past): If I had known about the exchange programme, I would have applied.

This means: I did NOT know about it, so I did NOT apply.

Fill in the Gaps

1 If the school a cultural awareness course, the students would have learned about stereotypes earlier.

2 If Maria had travelled to India last summer, she that her stereotypes were wrong.

3 The company the applicant if it had looked at his qualifications instead of his name.

4 If the film a more balanced picture, it would not have reinforced so many stereotypes.

5 If Tom had talked to his classmate from New Zealand, he that his assumptions were completely wrong.

6 The class the problem better if the teacher had used real-life examples.

7 If the journalist the facts, the article would not have been so one-sided.

8 If we had invited students from different countries to our school, we much more about their cultures.

Exercise D

Writing – Challenging Stereotypes

Write a paragraph (80–120 words) about one of the following topics. Use at least two passive voice sentences and one if-clause (type II or III) in your text.

Choose one topic

Topic 1: Think of a stereotype about Germans, or about people from another country you know. Is it fair? How could this stereotype be challenged? What would happen if people got to know each other better?

Topic 2: Imagine your school is starting an exchange programme with a school in a Commonwealth country (Canada, India, or New Zealand). How could this programme help students overcome stereotypes? What would students learn?

Useful vocabulary
Word bank stereotype prejudice discrimination cultural awareness assumption bias to challenge to overcome to judge exchange programme diversity open-minded
Your text
Aim for 80–120 words. Use at least 2 passive voice sentences and 1 if-clause.
